newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Hungarian share surge seen tailing off.
newsitem.headline: Hungarian share surge seen tailing off.

text.p: Hungarian shares maintained their record breaking pace on Wednesday to finish at a sixth successive closing high, but market participants believe the market was no longer cheap and some correction should come.
The BUX index ended at a preliminary 7,296.64 points, up 55.55 points or 0.77 percent.
The dollar's strengthening against the Hungarian currency to above 189 forints as well as expectations of good first half earnings reports drove the market higher.
"The market is going up because there isn't any bad news and everybody is anticipating good (second) quarter results," said Zsolt Madacsi of ING Barings.
Hungarian companies have to submit their first half earnings reports by August 15.
Traders said that Hungary's invitation to join NATO on Tuesday did not affect the market as expectations were already factored in prices, but they added that the move was important.

"This is political news, which raises the country's security factors," Madacsi said. "In assessing a country's macroeconomy, one has to take into consideration political risks and this (NATO invitation) reduces that risk."
On the futures market BUX contracts still firmed, but signalled the upper limits of the current rally, traders said.
"December BUX went to 8,000 points but had quite a lot of sellers at that level, so one could feel this was a technical limit," said Tamas Petheo of Buda-Cash Brokerhaz.
December BUX ended at 7,960 forints, compared to Tuesday's settlement price of 7,850.
ING Barings' Madacsi said he regarded the market as overvalued and expected a downward correction this month.
"We are on the edge...this will run into a correction."
On the longer-term, however, the market is well supported from the macroeconomic side, at least for this year, said Mark Precious, analyst at SBC Warburg in London.
"The macroeconomic support for the market remains pretty positive, we do see that being broadly on track at least through 1997," he said.
"There's more of a question mark in 1998 over how vigorous the authorities will be in...tightening fiscal policy in an election year."

He added, that while valuations were no longer cheap, and stocks were beginning to look fully valued, the market probably had a bit further to go on the back of positive macro news and partly because of concerns about the rest of Eastern Europe.
On Wednesday, the most actively traded chemicals TVK jumped to a new record high of 3,840 forints, but fell back to close at 3,710 forints, down 10.
OTP Bank also joined the bull run to a new record high of 6,000 forints, before closing at 5,860, up 100.
Hotel firm Danubius added 120 forints to finish at 5,860, while tinned food manufacturer Globus continued its recent surge to close at a new record high of 2,800 forints, up 300.
